title: Extreme heat and wildfire smoke: Operational vulnerabilities and workforce strain in California healthcare facilities
content:
by Maggie Jones, Anu Ramachandran, Annie B. Rosenthal, Mira Miles, Donya Zarrinnegar, Jen Monroe Zakaras, Noam Shimon, Arianne Teherani, Sheri D. Weiser

Background

Extreme heat and wildfire smoke events are increasing in frequency, severity, and geographic reach, placing compounding strain on healthcare systems and workers. Despite growing recognition of these events as public health threats, critical gaps persist in our understanding of how frontline healthcare providers perceive facility preparedness and operational impacts, their access to resources, and their experiences of these events.

Objective

To explore frontline healthcare provider knowledge of emergency preparedness plans and resource availability for extreme heat and wildfire smoke events, and to characterize their perceptions of how these events affect patients, staff, and clinical operations at healthcare facilities in the San Francisco Bay Area.

Methods

Semi-structured interviews with 29 healthcare providers were conducted between June 2023 and December 2024. Interviews were conducted remotely over Zoom, recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Analysis followed a hybrid inductive-deductive approach using Dedoose qualitative research software, with each transcript double coded by two investigators.

Results

Four themes emerged. First, infrastructural inadequacies, including insufficient cooling and ventilation, equipment failures, and unreliable backup power, create cascading impacts on patient safety, staff comfort, and operational efficiency that disproportionately affect emergency departments, urgent care settings, and community clinics. Second, healthcare workers, especially outdoor and safety-net clinic workers, experience significant physical, psychological, logistical, and caregiving burdens during these events. Third, health systems, many of which are already operating at or near capacity, experience substantial operational strain, driven by increased emergency department volumes and acuity, delayed discharges, and heightened cognitive demands on staff. Fourth, knowledge of facility emergency plans was limited and siloed among most respondents, with resource management frequently described as improvised and unsupported by clear institutional guidance.

Conclusions

Extreme heat and wildfire smoke events create compounding, systems-level threats to the functioning of Bay Area healthcare facilities that are inadequately addressed by current preparedness frameworks. Findings point to the need for climate-ready infrastructure, anticipatory staffing models, structured communication between leadership and frontline staff, and institutional recognition of the importance of preparing for these events.
